Ask your documents. Then teach a model.

Tejas Patel

16 October 2026

Source: vignettes/articles/introducing-0-4-0.Rmd
introducing-0-4-0.Rmd

dragonfarm 0.4.0 starts from your documents. Drop in PDFs, Word files, and web pages, ask them questions, and get answers that name the page they came from. When you want more, it turns the same documents into training data and fine-tunes a model on them. All from R, on your own machine, free.

Ask, and see the source

I gave it Costco’s 2024 annual report, all 76 pages, and asked two questions:

Question

Who is Costco’s independent registered public accounting firm?

Costco’s independent registered public accounting firm is KPMG LLP, located in Seattle, WA [1].

[1] Annual report, p. 68 › Item 14, Principal Accounting Fees and Services
Question

What was net cash used in investing activities in fiscal 2024?

Net cash used in investing activities in fiscal 2024 totaled $4,409 million [1].

[1] Annual report, p. 34 › Cash Flows from Investing Activities

Of thirteen factual questions about the report, it got twelve right. The thirteenth, a figure printed inside a map, it said the report does not cover, rather than guessing.

Six steps, one app

The app, step by step: drop in documents, ask them with sources, review generated questions, train, watch the loss, compare against the base model.
  1. Documents. Drop in PDFs, Word files, web pages, spreadsheets, or a whole folder.
  2. Ask. Get answers with numbered sources you can check.
  3. Teach. A model writes practice questions and answers from your documents. You keep the good ones.
  4. Train. Fine-tune a model on the pairs you kept.
  5. Monitor. Watch it learn.
  6. Try it. Put the tuned model next to the original, both answering from your documents.

Your documents never leave your machine. No GPU? dragonfarm can send the training to a free Colab or Kaggle GPU and bring the model back.

What you get

  • Answers you can check. Every answer names its file, page, and section.
  • An honest “not covered”. Ask about something the documents do not contain and the answer says so.
  • Training data you did not have to write. Most people who want to fine-tune have documents, not a table of questions and answers. dragonfarm writes that table for you to review.
  • A model that is yours. It runs on your machine and loads anywhere with standard tools.
  • The right model for your machine. An 8 GB laptop GPU runs a 7B model; smaller cards and CPUs get a smaller one, picked for you.

What we measured

The same questions, the same documents, four model sizes, one 8 GB laptop GPU, before any training:

Model Annual report: right of 23 R manuals: right of 32 Said “not covered” when true, of 20
0.5B 17 19 16
1.5B 19 28 20
3B 20 30 20
7B 23 31 20

And after training:

  • A 7B trained on R’s manuals stayed exactly as accurate and changed its manner: shorter answers, a source cited every time.
  • On support tickets, a model trained this way recalled 89 percent of the policy facts on tickets it had never seen, against 68 percent for ordinary fine-tuning. When the policy changed after training, it followed the new version in 88 percent of answers.
  • For a fixed format such as turning tickets into JSON, even the smallest model scored 20 of 20 after a few minutes of training.

The details are in Choosing a model size.

What it does not do

  • Questions that need every row of a spreadsheet (“which year had the highest margin?”) are better answered in R, on the data.
  • Scanned pages need OCR first, and numbers inside charts are lost.
  • Small models trained on a few hundred examples can become confident when they should not be. Review the training questions, and prefer a larger model for answering.
  • These numbers come from a handful of documents, not yours. Try it on yours.

Try it

dragonfarm reaches CRAN in November. Until then, get it from R-universe, which builds it for Windows, Mac, and Linux. Then open the app with dragon_app(), or follow the quickstart.

dragonfarm is MIT licensed. Issues, documents that break it, and pull requests are welcome at github.com/tejas4patel/dragonfarm, and there are a few good first issues to start from.
